Front: Why is `String` considered a reference type even though it is easy to write?
Back: Because a `String` variable stores a reference to a `String` object, not a primitive value.
Extra: String has special literal syntax, but it is still an object type. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/nutsandbolts/datatypes.html.

Front: Why should money usually not be stored with `float` or `double`?
Back: Floating-point types can have rounding errors and are not exact decimal types.
Extra: For money, Java developers often use `BigDecimal`. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/nutsandbolts/datatypes.html.

Front: What happens in integer division such as `5 / 2`?
Back: Java performs integer division and returns `2`.
Extra: Use `5 / 2.0` if you need `2.5`. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/nutsandbolts/datatypes.html.

Front: Why can narrowing casting lose data?
Back: The target type may not be able to represent all values or precision from the source type.
Extra: Example: `(int) 9.8` becomes `9`; the decimal part is lost. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/nutsandbolts/datatypes.html.

Front: Why does `byte c = a + b` fail when `a` and `b` are bytes?
Back: Java promotes small integer operands to `int` during arithmetic operations.
Extra: Use `int c = a + b`, or cast carefully if you truly need `byte`. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/nutsandbolts/datatypes.html.

Front: Why can `Integer boxed = null; int value = boxed;` fail?
Back: Java tries to unbox `boxed`, but unboxing `null` causes `NullPointerException`.
Extra: Wrappers can be null; primitives cannot. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/nutsandbolts/datatypes.html.

Front: What is the difference between `int` and `Integer`?
Back: `int` is a primitive type; `Integer` is a wrapper class and reference type.
Extra: `Integer` can be used in collections and can be `null`; `int` cannot be `null`. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/nutsandbolts/datatypes.html.

Front: Why is `"Java".equals(text)` often safer than `text.equals("Java")`?
Back: If `text` is null, `"Java".equals(text)` returns false, but `text.equals("Java")` throws `NullPointerException`.
Extra: This pattern is useful when the variable may be null. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/nutsandbolts/datatypes.html.

Front: Why should wrapper objects usually not be compared with `==`?
Back: `==` compares object references, not numeric value, for wrappers.
Extra: Use `.equals()` for wrapper value comparison unless you intentionally need reference comparison. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/nutsandbolts/datatypes.html.

Front: Why is `List<int>` invalid in Java?
Back: Generics require reference types, so collections use wrapper classes such as `Integer`.
Extra: Use `List<Integer>` instead. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/nutsandbolts/datatypes.html.

Front: Why is `double` the default choice for decimal literals?
Back: Java treats decimal literals such as `9.99` as `double` unless marked with `F`.
Extra: This is why `float price = 9.99;` does not compile without `F`. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/nutsandbolts/datatypes.html.

Front: Why is `char c = "A";` invalid?
Back: `"A"` is a String literal, not a char literal.
Extra: Use single quotes for char: `char c = 'A';`. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/nutsandbolts/datatypes.html.

Front: Why is `boolean valid = 1;` invalid in Java?
Back: Java does not convert `1` to `true` or `0` to `false`.
Extra: Boolean values must be `true` or `false`. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/nutsandbolts/datatypes.html.

Front: Why can fields have default values while local variables cannot be used unassigned?
Back: Fields are initialized by Java defaults, but local variables must be definitely assigned before use.
Extra: This prevents accidental use of uninitialized local data. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/nutsandbolts/datatypes.html.

Front: Why can changing an object through one reference affect another reference?
Back: Both references may point to the same object.
Extra: This is reference aliasing: two names can refer to one object. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/nutsandbolts/datatypes.html.

Front: Why is an array considered a reference type even if it stores primitives?
Back: The array itself is an object, and the variable stores a reference to that array object.
Extra: `int[] numbers` is a reference variable even though the array elements are `int`. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/nutsandbolts/datatypes.html.

Front: Why does `name.length()` fail if `name` is null?
Back: There is no String object to call the method on.
Extra: Calling an instance method on `null` causes `NullPointerException`. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/nutsandbolts/datatypes.html.

Front: Why does `(int) 9.8` become `9` instead of rounding to `10`?
Back: Narrowing from `double` to `int` truncates the decimal part.
Extra: Casting is not the same as mathematical rounding. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/nutsandbolts/datatypes.html.

Front: Why can `(byte) 130` produce an unexpected value?
Back: `byte` cannot represent all `int` values, so narrowing can overflow/wrap.
Extra: Narrowing conversion can lose information. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/nutsandbolts/datatypes.html.

Front: Why does `byte c = a + b;` fail when `a` and `b` are bytes?
Back: Arithmetic on small integer types is promoted to `int`.
Extra: The result of `a + b` is `int`, not `byte`. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/nutsandbolts/datatypes.html.

Front: Why can autoboxing be convenient but still risky?
Back: It reduces manual conversion, but wrappers can be null and may cause unboxing errors.
Extra: `Integer x = null; int y = x;` throws `NullPointerException`. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/nutsandbolts/datatypes.html.

Front: Why can `Integer a = 1000; Integer b = 1000; a == b` be false?
Back: `==` compares object references for wrappers, and these may be different objects.
Extra: Use `a.equals(b)` for value comparison. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/nutsandbolts/datatypes.html.

Front: Why is `"Java".equals(text)` null-safe?
Back: The string literal `"Java"` is not null, so calling `.equals()` on it is safe.
Extra: If `text` is null, the result is simply `false`. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/nutsandbolts/datatypes.html.
